tldr: Arhipov recaps lesser-known IntelliJ IDEA debugger features and shows a coding agent using them through a bundled debugger skill and MCP tools, gathering runtime evidence with logpoints instead of print statements.
summary: Arhipov starts from the point that breakpoints, value changes and HotSwap are JVM runtime capabilities exposed through a debugging protocol, so an agent can use them without a human at the IDE window. He walks through a run of features: Trace Stream Chain for visualising data flowing through a stream, method breakpoints on interface methods that stop in every implementation, wildcard method breakpoints that catch reflective calls, proxies and generated code, and logpoints, which are non-suspending breakpoints with an evaluated expression. He also shows a breakpoint that stays disabled until another one has been hit, so it only fires on a particular call path.

Each feature is then handed to an agent. IntelliJ IDEA bundles a debugger skill (installable into .agents/skills for a project) that tells the agent how and in what order to call the IDE's debugger tools through a single router MCP endpoint. Its principle is debugger-first, logpoint-first root cause analysis: collect evidence from logpoints and breakpoints rather than editing code with print lines. In the demos the agent finds a duplicate-keyboard bug caused by BigDecimal comparison in a stream, traces a 'never used' method to a reflective call through a non-constant method name, and reproduces a flaky concurrency test because its two logpoints add enough latency for both threads to pass the check-then-add.
keyPoints: Method breakpoints on an interface method stop in whichever implementation runs; wildcard class and method patterns also catch proxies, bytecode weaving and generated code.
A logpoint is a non-suspending breakpoint that evaluates and logs an expression; each output line links back to the source and can capture the stack trace.
The bundled IntelliJ debugger skill gives the agent a procedure, not just tools: reproduce the bug, place logpoints, collect evidence, then fix and remove the breakpoints.
Logpoints work in compiled third-party libraries, where the agent's usual print-statement habit is impossible.
For race conditions, logpoints (or a thread-only suspend policy) widen the timing window enough to make an intermittent failure reproduce on the first run.
takeaways: Enable the IntelliJ debugger skill for your project and tell the agent explicitly to debug, so it reaches for logpoints instead of println.
Use method breakpoints with wildcard patterns to find out who calls code that 'Find Usages' says is unused.
Try a breakpoint that stays disabled until another one is hit when you only care about one call path into a shared method.

quotes.text: Why do you think people add println statements instead of adding the breakpoint? Because it's very hard to figure out where you have to set the breakpoint.

chapters.title: Stream debugging and Trace Stream Chain

watchIf: You use coding agents in IntelliJ IDEA and want them to debug with runtime evidence instead of scattering print statements through your code.
